gpus.name: NVIDIA B300 SXM6 AC/PC (HGX B300, the board vast.ai lists as 'B300' / 'B300 PC')
gpus.architecture: Blackwell Ultra (2 reticle-sized dies, TSMC 4NP, 208B transistors)
gpus.notes: SMs: the full chip has 160 SMs. NVIDIA says 'Available SM count and HBM capacity varies by SKU.' A real B300 SXM6 AC reports '148 SMs (10.3)' (ricardojacomini STREAM log). Vast.ai's spec box says 20,480 CUDA cores (=160x128), which is the full-chip number, not the board it rents. Clock: 2032 MHz is the nvidia-smi max graphics clock on both AC and PC boards (gpuhunt PR, measured with nvidia-smi -q). It is a max, not a sustained clock. Cross-check: NVIDIA's HGX B300 FP32 spec is 600 TFLOPS / 8 GPUs = 75 TFLOPS. 75e12/(148 SM x 128 lanes x 2 flops) = 1.98 GHz, which agrees. Memory: nvidia-smi reports 275,040 MiB = 268.6 GiB = 288.4 GB, so vast.ai's '269 GB' is GiB. Bandwidth: NVIDIA gives 8 TB/s max. The ricardojacomini log reports 7,672 GB/s peak (3996 MHz x 7680-bit) and measured STREAM Triad at 6,851 GB/s with ECC on. Power: 1100 W limit in nvidia-smi on HGX/vast boards; 1400 W is the GB300 rack figure. L2: NOT FOUND in any primary source. It may be 126 MB like B200, but that is unverified. INT32 rates per SM per clock are from the CUDA 13.4 Best Practices Guide table, cc 10.3 column. They are the same as cc 8.9 (RTX 4090): add.s32 128; extended-precision add / 3-operand add 64; mad.lo.s32 64 (footnote: 32 for extended-precision, which I take to cover the carry and wide forms); shl 64; xor 64; clz 16; popc 16; bit reverse 64. min/max is 128, vs 64 on 8.9. int32_lanes_per_sm=64 is the logic/shift/IMAD width. Simple adds reach 128 because both pipes can take them. ARITHMETIC vs RTX 4090: per-SM rates are equal, so the ratio is SMs x clock. 148 x 2.032 = 300.7 SM-GHz, and the 4090 is 128 x 2.520 = 322.6, giving 0.932x. Using NVIDIA's FP32 peaks instead (same 128 FP32 lanes on both): 75/82.6 = 0.908x. IMAD/s = 300.7e9 x 64 = 19.2 T/s, vs 20.6 T/s for the 4090. So the 2^72 job (1.03 4090-years) takes about 1.03/0.932 = 1.10 B300-years, if per-clock IPC matches (estimate). What Blackwell Ultra changed vs B200 (does NOT matter for INT32): FP32:FP64 goes 64:1 (vs 2:1 on 10.0), and FP64 add is 2/clk/SM vs 64. HGX FP64 is 10 TFLOPS for 8 GPUs vs 296 on B200. INT8 tensor is 3 POPS vs 72. NVFP4 dense goes 15 vs 10 PF, SFU EX2 doubles (10.7 vs 5 TeraExp/s), HBM goes 288 vs 192 GB. FP32 is unchanged at 75 TF/GPU. One change that could matter: float-to-32-bit-int conversion drops to 2/clk/SM on SM > 10.0 (it is 16 on 10.0). That only matters if the kernel emits F2I. Vast.ai live API, 2026-10-16: 5 B300 offers, all at about $9.93/GPU-hour on-demand, 275040 MiB, cc 1030, 1100 W, hosts on CUDA 13.2 / driver 595. Only one host is verified. Software: CUDA 12.8 ptxas rejects sm_103 (ricardojacomini). sm_100 cubins run on 10.3 through binary compatibility.

gpus.name: NVIDIA B200 (HGX B200 SXM6)
gpus.architecture: Blackwell (2 dies x 80 SMs physical, 74 enabled per die)
gpus.notes: SMs: 'B200 enables 74 SMs per die, giving 148 SMs' (Chips and Cheese, measured on Verda B200s). Clock: 1965 MHz max graphics clock 'per the 8x B200 node capture' (NVIDIA k8s-test-infra NVML mock profile). Cross-checks: HGX FP32 600 TF / 8 = 75 TF per GPU (Lenovo: 75 TFLOPS), and 75e12/(148 x 256) = 1.98 GHz. Chips and Cheese measured L1D latency of 39 cycles = 19.6 ns, which also implies about 1.99 GHz in practice. L2: 126 MB (NVIDIA Blackwell Tuning Guide, stated for GB200; Chips and Cheese, B200). Memory: NVIDIA's HGX spec is '180 GB' (tuning guide: 'up to 180 GB'). Vast.ai B200s report 183,359 MiB = 179.1 GiB = 192.3 GB, so NVIDIA's 180 is really GiB. gpus.notes: Ada whitepaper: 128 SMs, 16384 CUDA cores, 2520 MHz boost, 82.6 FP32 TFLOPS, 41.3 'Peak INT32 TOPS' (= 128 x 64 x 2.52 GHz x 2, so it counts multiply-add as 2 ops), 73,728 KB L2, 24 GB, 1008 GB/s, 450 W TGP. datacenter-blackwell.caveats:
BOTTOM LINE (estimate): a B300 is not faster than an RTX 4090 for this kernel. NVIDIA's own per-SM per-clock integer table gives the same numbers for cc 8.9, 9.0, 10.0 and 10.3 (IMAD 64, wide/extended IMAD 32, shift/funnel 64, LOP 64, extended add 64, clz/popc/brev 16). So for this kernel the ratio is just SMs x clock. That makes the B300 about 0.91-0.93x a 4090, the B200 about 0.90x, and the H100/H200 about 0.81x per GPU, at rated/max clocks. Blackwell Ultra's changes (FP64 cut to 64:1, INT8 tensor cut, NVFP4 +50%, 2x SFU exp, 288 GB HBM) don't help INT32. The one possible penalty: F2I conversion is 2/clk/SM on SM > 10.0, which only matters if the kernel uses it.

COST, from the vast.ai public offers API on 2026-10-16, on-demand: B300 $9.93/GPU-h vs RTX 4090 median $0.469. The full 2^72 run would cost about 9,684 B300-hours x $9.93 = about $96k, vs 9,029 4090-hours x $0.469 = about $4.2k, roughly 23x more. A B300 only breaks even if the larger tables cut total GPU work by about 95% or more.

VRAM HEADROOM: assuming each extra lookahead bit doubles a power-of-two table, I can't verify that against your table layout. The largest power-of-two table that fits is 16 GiB on a 4090 (24,564 MiB) and 256 GiB on a B300 (275,040 MiB = 268.6 GiB). That is +4 doublings. B200 (179 GiB) and H200 (140 GiB) give +3, H100 (79.6 GiB) gives +2, and an RTX 5090 (32,607 MiB) gives +0. log2 of the capacity ratio is 3.49 for B300 vs 4090. You can judge from your measured gain per extra lookahead bit whether 4 doublings could come anywhere near a 23x cost gap.

UNCERTAINTIES:
(1) Clocks are nvidia-smi max values. B300's 2032 MHz is from a third-party nvidia-smi -q comparison; B200's 1965 MHz is from an NVIDIA NVML mock profile. Sustained clocks under your kernel are unknown. The 4090 may have run above 2.52 GHz during your 1.03-year measurement, which would make the datacenter cards look worse.
(2) NVIDIA's two throughput tables disagree. The CUDA 13.4 Best Practices Guide says add.s32 is 128 on all cc and min/max 128 on 9.0+. The CUDA 12.9.1 Programming Guide says int add 64 on 7.x-10.0 and min/max 64 through 10.0. Both list 8.9 and 10.x the same for IMAD, shift and logic, so the conclusion holds either way. Reading 'extended-precision' as covering 32x32->64 IMAD.WIDE is my interpretation.
(3) cc 9.0/10.x allow 64 resident warps per SM vs 48 on 8.9. That could help a latency-bound kernel, but not if it is limited by registers (all have 64K registers per SM).
(4) NOT FOUND in primary sources: B300 L2 size, GB300 enabled SM count, and an official NVIDIA boost clock for B200/B300 (NVIDIA doesn't publish one). H200 SM count, clock and L2 are inferred from H100.
(5) Vast.ai's static spec pages are unreliable. The B300 page claims 20,480 CUDA cores (the 160-SM full chip), but the SXM6 AC boards it rents report 148 SMs. The B200 page lists 96 GB and 1837 MHz, both wrong. Only 5 B300 offers existed and only 1 host was verified.
(6) A 1-hour benchmark of your kernel on a vast B300 (about $10) would replace all of these estimates with a measurement. Build for sm_100 or sm_103: CUDA 12.8 ptxas rejects sm_103, sm_100 cubins run on 10.3, and the vast hosts report CUDA 13.2. I did not research the RTX 5090 here (cc 12.0, 40 vast offers, median $0.614/h).

gpus.name: GeForce RTX 5090
gpus.notes: L2 is 96 MB (98,304 KB), not the full GB202's 128 MB. The whitepaper says so in prose and in the table. It has 170 of 192 SMs. INT32 on all 128 lanes? An NVIDIA engineer on the team that owns the throughput table (forum, June 2025) said IMAD, LOP3, PRMT and IADD3 are NOT improved on Blackwell. Only 2-operand IADD, IMNMX and ISETP/FSETP got faster. For an IMAD-bound kernel, expect per-SM-per-clock rate equal to the 4090. other-gpus.caveats:
1. IMAD throughput is the same per SM per clock on every card listed. NVIDIA's current table (CUDA C++ Best Practices Guide 13.4, Table 5, updated Oct 12, 2026) gives 32-bit mad.lo at 64 results/clk/SM for cc 7.5, 8.0, 8.6/8.9, 9.0, 10.0, 10.3 and 12.0/12.1, with footnote "32 for extended-precision". The same holds for extended-precision add/subtract and 3-operand add (64), 32-bit shift (64), AND/OR/XOR (64), and clz and popc (16). __ffs is usually brev + flo, and the older 12.9.1 table lists bit reverse at 16, so expect it at quarter rate everywhere. Funnel shift has no row of its own; I assume it runs at the shift rate, which is an inference. For a kernel bound by IMAD, carry chains, LOP3 and shifts, per-card throughput therefore scales with SM count times sustained clock.
2. The 'INT32 on all 128 lanes' claim for GB202 (RTX 5090, RTX PRO 6000) mostly doesn't apply to this kernel. The whitepapers say the cores are unified and integer throughput doubles for 'many' instructions. However, an NVIDIA engineer on the team that owns the throughput table stated (forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/blackwell-integer/320578, June 2025) that IMAD, LOP3, PRMT and IADD3 are not improved. Only 2-operand IADD, IMNMX/VIMNMX and ISETP/FSETP are faster. Forum users measured RTX 5090 IMAD at about 52.4 TOPS (half the whitepaper's 104.8), and RTX 5080 IMAD at the same per-SM rate as the RTX 4080. The CUDA 12.9.0 guide briefly appeared to list doubled IMAD for 12.x; the 12.9.1 archive and 13.x tables show 64. Third-party pages quoting 2x INT32 should not be trusted for IMAD.
3. Also relevant to the B300 question: the same table gives cc 10.0 (B200) and 10.3 (B300) 64 IMAD/clk/SM and 64 LOP/shift. Datacenter Blackwell has no per-SM integer advantage, so its value here is VRAM only. Its per-SM rate matches the 4090, and its SM count and clock decide everything else (not researched here).
4. The GPU-year estimates are MY ESTIMATES. They scale your measured 1.03 GPU-years on the 4090 by (SMs x spec boost clock) / (128 x 2.52 GHz). They ignore power-limited sustained clocks, which matters most for the 300 W RTX 6000 Ada and Max-Q, the capped Server Edition and the PCIe datacenter cards. They also ignore occupancy and L2 or memory effects; a mostly-random 132-byte read per thread into a table much larger than L2 should make L2 size secondary.
5. Gaps. RTX PRO 6000 Server Edition: L2 and boost clock are not published (2.49 GHz derived from 120 TFLOPS; L2 left null, likely 128 MB). L40S: L2 not in any L40S document (96 MB inferred from the L40). The H100 SM count and INT32 cores come from a preliminary whitepaper hosted by a third party. RTX PRO whitepaper Table 1 gives the RTX 6000 Ada 1008 GB/s, but its appendix and the datasheet give 960.
6. vast.ai prices could not be retrieved. The per-GPU pages render offers client-side and showed 'No current offers' in static HTML, and the public API returned 403. vast.ai uses the type names RTX 4090, RTX 5090, RTX PRO 6000 WS, RTX PRO 6000 S, RTX 6000Ada, L40S, RTX 3090, A100 SXM4, A100 PCIE and H100 PCIE. Its own spec blurbs contain errors: the Server Edition is shown as 2617 MHz and 1.79 TB/s, and the A100 PCIE description says 40 GB. vast.ai's B300 page says 288 GB HBM3e; the ~269 GB figure from the listing does not appear there.

(Number of Results per Clock Cycle per Multiprocessor)': https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-best-practices-guide/index.html#throughput-of-native-arithmetic-instructions (8.6 and 8.9 share one column since BPG 13.3)
rows.notes: Table rows used: 'add.f32' 128; 'add.s32' 128 (two-operand add only); 'extended-precision add/sub, 3-operand addition' 64; 'mad.lo.s32' 64, footnote 6: '32 for extended-precision'; 'shl.b32' 64; 'clz.b32' 16; 'popc.b32' 16; 'xor.b32' 64; 64-bit add 32; min/max 64. The table has no funnel-shift row. The 64 comes from the shift row: nvcc 13.1 compiles both << and __funnelshift_r to the same SHF instruction (inferred, not documented). The table has no __ffs row either: __ffs compiles to BREV + FLO.U32.SH, two instructions (see the 8.9 measured row). The older Programming Guide table (CUDA 12.9.1) gave 8.6 as 64 for 'add, extended-precision add', 64 for IMAD and 16 for bit reverse. CUDA 13.0 'corrected entries for integer arithmetic'.

rows.notes: Every integer and FP32 row is the same as 8.6. As there, 128 is for two-operand add.s32; IADD3, 3-operand and extended (carry) adds are 64. IMAD is 64, or 32 for extended precision. Funnel shift = shift row (inferred from SASS). CUDA 12.9.1 Programming Guide (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/12.9.1/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#arithmetic-instructions) gave 64 for 32-bit integer add on 8.9.

rows.source: Local microbenchmark: /tmp/claude-1000/-home-ryan-Projects-Collatz-distributed/020acebb-4e99-4cf9-93cf-c5a23320f639/scratchpad/cuda/tput.cu. Uses inline PTX; SASS checked with cuobjdump; rate per SM = clock64 span of that SM; full occupancy (48 warps/SM).
rows.notes:
Measured on an otherwise idle GPU (desktop compositor only):
- IMAD: 63.9
- IMAD.WIDE.U32 (32x32->64, mul.wide.u32): 31.9 (half rate)
- IMAD.HI.U32: 31.9 (half rate)
- IADD3 instructions: about 64. ptxas fuses pairs of two-operand add.u32 into one IADD3, so the PTX-level rate is 126 adds/clk.
- add.cc + addc (IADD3 + IADD3.X): 64
- SHF.R.W (funnel shift) 63.6; SHF.L 63.3; LOP3 63.3; IMNMX 63.3
- FLO = POPC = BREV = MUFU.EX2 = 16
- __ffs-style BREV + FLO.SH pair: 8 per clk, i.e. BREV and FLO share one 16/clk unit.
Two things to know about these numbers:

instruction-throughput.blackwell_int32_note:
No. Per SM per clock, Blackwell kept the same IMAD rate as Ada and Hopper: 64 results/clk/SM, or 32 for extended-precision forms. On the 4090 I measured IMAD.WIDE.U32 and IMAD.HI.U32 at 32. Only a few simple integer instructions got faster, and only on consumer Blackwell (12.0). Datacenter Blackwell (10.0 B200, 10.3 B300) shows no INT32 change from Hopper.

Evidence:
1) Current CUDA C++ Best Practices Guide 13.4, Table 5 (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-best-practices-guide/index.html#throughput-of-native-arithmetic-instructions):
- 32-bit IMAD is 64 for every column from 7.5 to 12.0/12.1, including 10.0 and 10.3.
- Shift and LOP3 are 64 everywhere, clz/popc 16 everywhere, and 3-operand/extended add 64 everywhere.
- 10.0 and 10.3 have the same integer entries as 9.0.
- 12.0 differs only in 64-bit add (64 vs 32), vote (128 vs 64), and sad/vabsdiff4 (halved to 32).
2) NVIDIA employee mjoux, who says he is on the team that owns this table, 2025-06-11 (https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/blackwell-integer/320578/137): on Blackwell 'some instructions have not been improved/changed: this applies to IMAD, LOP3, PRMT for example, as well as IADD3. The main improved instructions … are IADD, IMNMX/VIMNMX, FSETP/ISETP: addition of 2 operands and min/max/compare.' He adds that earlier architectures could already reach 2x add throughput by mixing IADD3 with IMAD.IADD/VIADD, and that 12.0 does it with one instruction.
3) NVIDIA moderator 'Greg' (staff, group Employee), 2025-11-05 (https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/integer-ntt-on-rtx-20xx-a100-vs-rtx-30xx-40xx-50xx/350124/10): 'For a kernel that is 50% IMAD and 50% INT32 Volta - GB20x have the same instruction throughput.'
4) RTX Blackwell whitepaper v1.1 (https://images.nvidia.com/aem-dam/Solutions/geforce/blackwell/nvidia-rtx-blackwell-gpu-architecture.pdf, p.12):
- It says GB20x 'fully unif[ies] the INT32 cores with the FP32 cores', but 'the unified cores can only operate as either FP32 or INT32 cores in any given clock cycle. While many common INT operations can run at up to 2x throughput, not all INT operations can attain 2x speedups', and it refers readers to the CUDA guide.
- Its Table 3 'Peak INT32 TOPS' (4090 41.3, 5090 104.8, equal to FP32 TFLOPS) is a marketing peak. It is not the IMAD rate.
5) Datacenter Blackwell:
- The Blackwell Ultra blog only says each SM has '128 CUDA Cores for FP32 and INT32 operations' (https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/inside-nvidia-blackwell-ultra-the-chip-powering-the-ai-factory-era).
- The Blackwell Tuning Guide (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/blackwell-tuning-guide/index.html) says nothing about INT32 throughput.
- I found no primary source claiming an INT32 or IMAD rate change on 10.0 or 10.3.

What this means for whole-GPU speed (estimate): it scales only with SM count × clock.
- RTX 4090: 128 SMs × 64 × 2.52 GHz boost (Ada/RTX Blackwell whitepaper table) ≈ 20.6 T IMAD/s.
- RTX 5090: 170 × 64 × 2.407 GHz ≈ 26.2 T IMAD/s.
- B300: NVIDIA gives only 'up to 160 SMs'. Third-party sites (unverified) list about 75 FP32 TFLOPS, which implies about 1.8–2.0 GHz, so roughly 18–20 T IMAD/s. That is about a 4090, and its extra VRAM adds no integer throughput.
instruction-throughput.caveats:
1) Where the table lives now: the CUDA C++ Programming Guide no longer has the table. docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide now redirects to the new 'CUDA Programming Guide' (Release 13.4.2, Sep 10, 2026). Its Table 30 footnote says 'For more information on throughput see the CUDA Best Practices Guide'. Since CUDA 13.0 the authoritative table is BPG Table 5.

2) The BPG warns that these are 'max theoretical throughput' figures that 'may only be achieved via specific sequences of instructions'.

3) Values have changed between doc versions:
- The 12.9 Programming Guide gave 64 for integer add on 8.x/9.0/10.0 and 128 on 12.0.
- BPG 13.x gives 128 for two-operand add on every CC, and 64 for IADD3 and extended add.
- Min/max for 9.0/10.0 went from 64 (BPG 13.0–13.2) to 128 (13.3 and later).
- The 10.3 column first appears in BPG 13.3.

4) Rows the table does not have:
- Funnel shift: my 64 is an inference. nvcc 13.1 compiles both << and __funnelshift_r to SHF on sm_89, sm_100, sm_103 and sm_120, and the shift row is 64.
- __ffs: it is BREV + FLO.U32.SH. On sm_89 that measured 8 per clk per SM, half the 16 for clz.
- The current 'bit reverse: not.b32 = 64' row looks mislabeled. BREV measured 16 on sm_89, as the old table says.

5) The 32-bit multiply-add question: your 32x32->64 multiply-add compiles to IMAD.WIDE.U32, which measured 32/clk/SM (half rate) on the 4090. The docs' footnote '32 for extended-precision' probably covers this, but they never say so explicitly. I could not measure 9.0, 10.x or 12.0, because the only local GPU is the 4090.

6) Your kernel's instruction mix (estimate). These counts come from a static SASS count of a copy of cuda/kernel.cu, snapshotted around 15:36. The file had been changed at 15:31, so it may have changed since.
- Fast-path hot loop per iteration (2 odd + 2 even runs): about 118 instructions on sm_89, 109 on sm_100/103, 107 on sm_120.
- That loop contains 6 IMAD.WIDE.U32, 2 IMAD, 16 SHF, 4 BREV, 4 FLO, about 17 ISETP, about 7 LOP3, plus IADD3/IADD and moves.
- On sm_89, rough pipe costs per thread-iteration: issue about 0.92 SM-clk, ALU pipe about 0.9, FMA/IMAD pipe about 0.58, BREV/FLO unit about 0.5.
- So the kernel looks issue/ALU-bound, not IMAD-bound. That means 12.0's faster IADD/ISETP could help somewhat, and 10.x would not help at all.

7) A possible bottleneck in the kernel: THREEPOWERSU16 is a __constant__ array indexed by a per-thread value (LDC.U16 c[0x3][R]). Constant-cache reads with different addresses in one warp are serialized. This may cost more than the arithmetic. I have not measured it.

8) B300 figures:
- vast.ai's '~269 GB' is probably NVIDIA's 288 GB (decimal) shown in GiB (288e9 B ≈ 268.2 GiB). That is my inference.
- B300 clock, enabled SM count and FP32 TFLOPS come only from third-party sites (flopper.io, spheron, etc.) and do not agree with each other. NVIDIA says SM count varies by SKU.
- The vast.ai B300 article (Jun 3, 2026) gives 160 SMs and 288 GB but no clock or price.

9) My microbenchmark has one artifact: with more than about 6 outstanding FLO/BREV/POPC/MUFU ops per warp, the 6 scoreboards alias and the observed rate halves. The rates I report come from runs below that limit (chains 1–6), where they were stable.

verdicts.reasoning:
I could not confirm the vast.ai numbers from independent press. Two aggregators showed vast.ai B300 at $8.69 and from $9.80; I could not tie either to a timestamp, so I relied on vast.ai's own data.

1. I downloaded the vast.ai public feed myself. Every feed-derived number the researcher reported matches exactly: p10, median, min, available, vram_gb, and the daily medians for 10-15 and 07-18. I also read vast.ai's own page code ([gpu] JS chunk). The vast.ai/pricing/gpu/<GPU> pages fetch this exact JSON and show current.min as the headline "Lowest hourly price" and current.median as "Median hourly price". So the feed is the provider's displayed price.

2. I queried the live bundles API myself, for both on-demand and bid, paging by price to get past the 64-offer cap. The B300 picture is confirmed exactly: two hosts, UK 8x unverified at $9.93 with min bid $7.50, Croatia 1x verified at $9.9375 with min bid $4.875, gpu_ram 275040 MiB. My per-offer median for B300 ($9.9307) equals the feed median, which suggests the feed takes its median over offers, not over GPUs.

3. Corrections, most important first:
   - B200: the feed's $6.25 on-demand low is stale. Live on-demand is $9.00 to $9.38, and the researcher's own 20:28Z check had already seen this. Using $6.25 as an on-demand price understates the B200 by about 30%.
   - H100 SXM: the feed's $1.734 low is likewise not rentable now; the live low is about $2.14. The interruptible $0.654 minimum has disappeared; the live minimum is $1.00, from a host with reliability 0.633.
   - RTX PRO 6000 WS interruptible: p10 is now $0.87 to $0.97, not $0.733.
   - Host counts differ slightly: B200 is 3 machines on 2 hosts, not 3 hosts.
   - The 4090 and 5090 interruptible minimums ($0.12 and $0.273) are thin outliers that move from minute to minute.

4. Caveats the researcher did not state:
   - The feed's daily "median" series uses an undocumented basis. It runs well below the current listing medians: L40S $0.35 vs $0.64, RTX PRO 6000 S $1.00 vs $1.40, 5090 $0.56 vs $0.75. So the "daily median" and "current median" numbers should not be compared as the same statistic.
   - Prices change within minutes, and B300 supply is only 9 GPUs. The UK listing expires 2026-10-21, so at about 1 GPU-year of work, B300 availability on vast.ai cannot be counted on.
   - Interruptible instances are paused when someone outbids you or an on-demand renter arrives. The data is kept, but the instance stops running (vast docs).

5. RunPod's B300 and B200 prices are confirmed by an independent aggregator, and NVIDIA's DGX B300 guide confirms 288 GB per GPU.

key_uncertainties: Clocks. Only the RTX 4090 has been measured. Every other figure is SMs x clock scaling on NVIDIA's theoretical per-SM table, so treat each ratio as uncertain by about 10-15%. A 1-hour benchmark of the real kernel would replace these estimates: about $10 on a vast B300, under $2 on a 5090 or PRO 6000. `cv measure --n 72 --gpu` already does this.

Which clock the 1.03 GPU-year baseline ran at is unknown. The 4090 is rated at 2.52 GHz, but GeForce cards typically sustain about 2.68-2.75 GHz. The verifiers corrected the B300 ratio for this, from 0.932 to about 0.87. I applied the same correction to the other datacenter parts (L40S, A100, H100, H200, B200, GB300) because their listed clock is a hard maximum. This extension is my own estimate. I left GeForce and workstation cards at their rated boost, on the assumption that they overshoot it in proportion to the 4090; that assumption is unverified. If the 4090 really ran at 2.52 GHz, the datacenter rows rise by about 7.7% (B300 becomes 0.93).

The kernel may not be purely IMAD-bound. A static SASS count suggests it is limited by instruction issue and the ALU pipe, with IMAD.WIDE at 32/clk and BREV/FLO at 16/clk. NVIDIA's table gives identical per-SM rates for all of these on cc 8.6, 8.9, 9.0, 10.0 and 10.3, so the SMs x clock scaling holds. On cc 12.0 parts (5090, PRO 6000), 2-operand IADD/ISETP run at 2x, which could add 0-15% per SM-clock (estimate). The constant-cache lookup THREEPOWERSU16 (LDC with divergent addresses) is an unmeasured possible bottleneck. The 64 resident warps per SM on 9.0/10.x, vs 48 on 8.9, help only if the kernel is latency-bound and not register-limited.

VRAM vs the lookahead window. This assumes the layout in COST_MODEL.md: two 2^B-bit arrays per class, one class per launch. On that basis VRAM does not limit a 24 GB 4090 until about B=36 (2 x 8 GiB). Larger cards add: B=37 at 48 GB, B=38 at 80-96 GB (A100/H100/PRO 6000), B=39 at 141-179 GiB (H200/B200), and B=40 on the B300 (2 x 128 GiB in 268.6 GiB). So the B300 buys only 4 more bits than a 4090, which itself still has about 8 bits of headroom over today's B=28. L2 starts limiting much earlier. B=28 (2 x 32 MB) fits the 4090's 72 MB L2, but B>=30 exceeds the L2 on every card listed (largest 126-128 MB). Beyond that, lookups go to DRAM on every GPU, and HBM bandwidth barely matters for a 132-byte read followed by microseconds of compute. Building the tables at B=36-40 (2^36-2^40 entries) and the host RAM and transfer that requires are not estimated. If all classes had to be resident at once, the limits drop by about 4 bits.

Cost implication (estimate). At $11.48 per 4090-equivalent hour against $0.509 for a 4090, the B300 is about 22.5x as expensive per unit of INT32 work. Larger tables would have to cut total GPU work by about 95.6% to break even. The full 2^72 run (about 9,029 4090-hours) comes to roughly $104k on B300s, against $4.6k on 4090s, $4.2k on 3090s, $5.4k on 5090s and $8.7k on PRO 6000s. Even interruptible B300 at $4.875 is about $5.63 per 4090-equivalent hour, about 11x a 4090. The PRO 6000 (96 GB, about $0.96 per 4090-equivalent hour) is the only large-VRAM option within about 2x of 4090 cost.
